posts.title: Relatable: "The ad worked." Which part?
posts.caption:
"The ad worked." Lovely. Which part?

The first shot? The line the creator opened with? The offer? Payday?

Nobody is wrong for not knowing. A results sheet tells you which ad won. It does not tell you why.

One habit you can start on Monday: before the next brief, finish this sentence in writing. "It worked because ___."

If the blank stays empty, you have just found your next test.

Save this for your Monday review. Follow @galvor.ai for more on reading your own ads.

posts.title: Monday review: add one line to the agenda
posts.hook: Most Monday ad reviews answer "how much?" and stop there.
posts.caption:
Most Monday ad reviews answer "how much?" and stop there.

Spend. RoAS. Top ad. Next week's launches. All useful, and all about last week.

Try adding two lines to the same agenda tomorrow:

One thing last week's ads taught us.
One thing we will do differently because of it.

It takes five minutes. Write both lines in the same doc every week, and in three months you have something a dashboard cannot give you: a memory.

What is the first question in your Monday review? Tell us below.

Follow @galvor.ai for more.

posts.title: Relatable: sale week makes every ad look good
posts.hook: Sale week: every ad looks like a winner.
posts.caption:
Sale week: every ad looks like a winner.

The week after is when you find out which ones were good and which ones were standing next to a big discount.

Before you crown anything from this week's numbers, do one small thing. Pick your top three sale ads and write down what each one had besides the offer: the first shot, the person, the message.

Then watch those three at full price. The ones that still hold are your real learning from the sale.

Save this for Monday. Follow @galvor.ai for more.

posts.title: Data drop: one brand's creative diversity score, 63 to 92
posts.hook: One brand's creative diversity score went from 63 to 92 out of 100.
posts.caption:
One brand's creative diversity score went from 63 to 92 out of 100.

That was two months after it made the changes Galvor recommended. It is one brand, so treat it as a signal and not a promise.

What the score is asking: are your ads different from each other, or the same ad in new colours?

A quick check you can run today. Put the first frames of your live ads side by side. Count how many you could tell apart with the sound off. If the honest answer is two, you are running two ads.

Source: Decoded #3 by Galvor. Follow @galvor.ai for more.

posts.title: Relatable: feedback, translated
posts.hook: "Make it pop." We have all said it. Nobody can act on it.
posts.caption:
"Make it pop." We have all said it. Nobody can act on it.

Vague feedback is usually a real feeling in a hurry. The person is right that something is off. They just have not said where.

A simple format that saves a round of edits. Every note gets three parts:

Where: the second it happens.
What: the thing on screen.
Change: what you want instead.

"Make it pop" becomes "at 0:02, show the product before the logo." Your editor and your creator can do that today.

Send this to the person who reviews your ads. Follow @galvor.ai for more.

posts.title: What 2026 taught us about new ads
posts.hook: What a year of reading ads taught us, in four lines.
posts.caption:
What a year of reading ads taught us, in four lines.

We studied the new video ads launched by brands we work with. Four patterns kept showing up:

A proven message in a new look did better than a new message over a familiar first shot.
New ads that looked like the ones already running got less spend.
Launching a batch of look-alikes together made it worse.
Some styles start expensive and settle close to average, so judge them slowly.

Thank you to every brand, creator and reader who learned with us this year.

Which line would you add? Follow @galvor.ai for more.

posts.title: Relatable: the year-end deck
posts.hook: The year-end deck: 40 slides on what happened. One missing slide on why.
posts.caption:
The year-end deck: 40 slides on what happened. One missing slide on why.

We have all built this deck. The charts are right. The numbers tie. And the first question in the room is still "so what do we do in January?"

One slide answers it. Three headings:

What we would repeat.
What we would stop.
What we still do not know.

Put it second, right after the title. The third heading is the brave one, and it usually gets the best discussion.

Save this before you open the deck. Follow @galvor.ai for more.

posts.title: Relatable: last week of December, and one calm job
posts.hook: Last week of December, marketing edition.
posts.caption:
Last week of December, marketing edition.

The out-of-office is on. The ads are not. And "let's pick this up in January" has been said with full confidence at least once.

If you do one calm job this week, make it this: rename your ads.

Pick one pattern and use it everywhere. Product, message, format, creator, month. In that order, every time.

It is dull work. It is also the reason next year you can sort a whole account by message and see what carried it.

Tag the teammate who names files "final_v3". Follow @galvor.ai for more.

posts.title: The question to ask before every brief
posts.hook: Before the next brief goes out, ask one question: what will this ad teach us?
posts.caption:
Before the next brief goes out, ask one question: what will this ad teach us?

Most briefs say what to make. Very few say what the team wants to find out.

So add one line at the top of the brief:

"We are testing whether ___ works better than ___."

A new opening line against the old one. A founder on camera against a customer. One blank each, nothing more.

Now the ad has a job even if it loses. A losing ad that answers the question still makes the next one better.

Save this for your next brief. Follow @galvor.ai for more.

posts.title: Relatable: the brief vs the feedback
posts.hook: The brief said "test a new opening". The feedback said "can the logo be bigger?"
posts.caption:
The brief said "test a new opening". The feedback said "can the logo be bigger?"

It happens on every team, ours included. By the time the video comes back, three weeks have passed and nobody has the brief open.

So the ad gets judged on taste, and the thing it was made to test gets edited out.

A small fix: paste the brief's goal as the first line of the feedback doc. Then sort every note into two piles. Notes that help the test. Notes that are just preference.

Do the first pile. Park the second.

Follow @galvor.ai for more.

posts.title: Be honest: how does your team decide which ad to cut?
posts.hook: Be honest. How does your team decide which ad to cut?
posts.caption:
Be honest. How does your team decide which ad to cut?

1. Gut feel
2. Worst number last week
3. A rule we wrote down
4. Whoever spoke last in the meeting

No wrong answers. Many teams are a mix.

One reason to move towards 3: in our analysis, some ad styles started about 35% dearer per order in their first two months and ended close to average over their life. Cut on week one and you never see that.

So write the rule before launch: how long, and against which number.

Comment your number. Follow @galvor.ai for more.

Source: Galvor analysis, ads launched May to Sep 2026.

posts.title: February check-in: which creative resolutions survived January?
posts.hook: First week of February. Time for an honest check-in.
posts.caption:
First week of February. Time for an honest check-in.

Which of these made it through January on your team?

One change per test.
Ads judged in weeks, not days.
Learnings written down where people can find them.
New ideas, not the same ad in new colours.

If your score is one out of four, you are in good company. Resolutions rarely fail because people stop caring. They fail because they never got a slot in the diary.

So pick one, and give it a recurring half hour every second week.

Tell us your score out of four. Follow @galvor.ai for more.
